levels.title: Merge Market
levels.story: At the Merge Market, two stalls each keep their goods sorted by price. Printer Pell shows Kit how to combine them into one sorted line without ever starting again from scratch.

everyday.scene: Two friends each hold a stack of exam papers sorted by name. You have to put them into one sorted stack.
everyday.question: Do you need to look through every paper each time?
everyday.answer: No. You only compare the top paper of each stack, take the earlier one, and repeat. That simple move is called merging.

lessons.title: Merging two sorted rows
text: Merging combines two sorted rows into one. Look at the front crate of each row, move the smaller to the output, and repeat. When one row is empty, move everything left in the other row.
Each comparison puts one crate into the output, so merging rows of sizes m and n takes at most m + n − 1 comparisons. The final merge in our example, 4 crates and 4, took 7.

terms.meaning: Combine two sorted rows into one sorted row.

predict.prompt: Two sorted rows of 5 crates each are merged. At most how many comparisons?

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 1: Recursion

lessons.title: Split, then merge
text: Mergesort uses divide and conquer. Split the row into two halves, sort each half by calling mergesort on it, then merge the two sorted halves. A row of one crate is already sorted, which is the base case.
Our eight crates split into 4 and 4, then 2 and 2, then 1 and 1. Merging back up takes 7 merges, with 17 comparisons in total, far under the 28 comparisons of a one-by-one method like selection sort.

terms.meaning: Split a problem into smaller copies, solve each, and combine the answers.

predict.prompt: What is the base case of mergesort?
predict.answer: A row of one crate (or none): it is already sorted.

lessons.title: Why it is fast
text: Halving 1,024 crates takes 10 levels to reach single crates. Each level of merging touches every crate once, so each level costs about n item-moves. The total is about n × log₂ n.
For 1,024 crates, that is about 10,240 item-moves. Selection sort needs about 523,776 comparisons. As n grows the gap widens: n log n grows much slower than n × n.

predict.prompt: Doubling the number of crates adds how many levels?

deeper.title: Memory cost
text: Merging usually needs extra room to hold the output, about as big as the row. This is the price mergesort pays for its steady speed.

fieldNotes.title: Merging in the real world
fieldNotes.text: Merging is useful whenever sorted pieces must be combined, for example when a big file is too large for memory: it is sorted in pieces that fit, and the sorted pieces are then merged.

summary: You merged two sorted halves by comparing fronts, saw mergesort split and merge its way to a sorted row, and linked its cost to log₂ n levels of n item-moves.
Pell stamps the crate. "One stack, in order." Next, a faster-looking method with a risk.

mistake.title: Merging rows that are not sorted
mistake.text: Merging only works if both halves are already sorted. That is why mergesort sorts each half before merging.

levels.title: Pivot Point
levels.story: Dock Clerk Dot is back, and this time she sorts a whole warehouse by picking a pivot crate and splitting the pile around it. It works astonishingly fast, unless the pivot is unlucky.

everyday.scene: You sort a pile of books by height: you pick one book, put shorter ones left, taller ones right, then do the same to each pile.
everyday.question: What if the book you pick is always the shortest one?
everyday.answer: Then one pile is empty every time, and you hardly make progress. How good the split is decides everything.

lessons.title: Partition, then repeat
text: Quicksort is divide and conquer with the hard work done before the split. Choose a pivot, partition the row so smaller crates sit on its left and bigger on its right, and the pivot is in its final place. Then sort the left part and the right part the same way.

There is no merging at the end, because partitioning already put the pieces in the right places. Our eight crates 35, 12, 48, 7, 29, 20, 41, 16 take 18 comparisons in total, using the last crate of each part as the pivot.

terms.meaning: The crate everything else is compared to in one partition.

predict.prompt: After a partition, where is the pivot?

lessons.title: Good and bad splits
text: If every pivot lands near the middle, the row halves each time. There are about log₂ n levels, each costing about n comparisons, so quicksort needs about n × log₂ n. This is the good case.

If the pivot always lands at an end, one side is empty, and each level removes only one crate. That is n − 1 comparisons, then n − 2, and so on: n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 in total, which is 45 for 10 crates. With the last crate as pivot, an already sorted row is exactly this bad case.

predict.prompt: A row is already sorted, and the pivot is always the last crate. How does the partition split?
predict.answer: Everything is smaller than the pivot, so the left side holds all the other crates and the right side is empty.

lessons.title: Choosing a pivot
text: Because bad luck is costly, real programs choose pivots more carefully: a random crate, or the middle of the first, middle and last. A random pivot makes the bad case very unlikely, whatever order the crates arrive in.
Quicksort's average cost is about n × log₂ n, and it sorts in place without needing extra space for the whole row. That is why it has been popular, even though mergesort has a better worst case.

predict.prompt: Why choose the pivot at random instead of always the last crate?
predict.answer: So that no particular input order can reliably make it slow.

deeper.title: Equal values
text: Rows with many equal crates can make a simple partition unbalanced. Careful versions handle equal crates separately.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 1: Recursion

fieldNotes.title: Quicksort in libraries
fieldNotes.text: Quicksort, or a variant such as introsort, is used in the standard library sorts of some languages, for example in some C++ implementations. Introsort starts with quicksort and switches to heapsort when the recursion gets too deep, which protects it against bad luck.

summary: You watched quicksort partition and repeat, saw that a pivot at the end of a sorted row is the worst case, and met the idea of choosing pivots at random.
Dot grins. "Fast on average, risky if careless." The next level gives a way to describe all these costs.

mistake.title: Calling quicksort always fast
mistake.text: Its average is about n × log₂ n, but with unlucky pivots it takes about n × n ÷ 2 comparisons. Both numbers are correct, for different inputs.

levels.title: Master's Riddle
levels.story: A wise old sailor won't give Kit the key to the harbour until Kit can answer a riddle: if a plan splits its job into pieces, how much work is the plan in total? There is a tidy rule for it.

everyday.scene: A manager splits a job between 2 helpers, each doing half. Each helper does the same, and splitting and joining costs a little work at each step.
everyday.question: How would you work out the total?
everyday.answer: Draw the helpers as a tree, add the work on each level, then add the levels. The Master Theorem is a shortcut for exactly that sum.

lessons.title: A plan as an equation
text: A divide-and-conquer plan can be written as a recurrence: T(n) = a × T(n/b) + f(n). It reads: to solve size n, solve a smaller copies each of size n/b, and then spend f(n) on splitting and combining.
Mergesort has a = 2 pieces, each half the size (b = 2), and spends about n on merging, so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Binary search has a = 1, b = 2, and constant work: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1.

terms.meaning: An equation that gives the cost of a problem using the cost of smaller ones.

predict.prompt: Mergesort splits into how many pieces, each what fraction of the size?
predict.answer: Two pieces, each half the size.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 1: Recursion

lessons.title: Add the levels
text: Draw the recursion as a tree. Level k has aᵏ pieces, each of size n/bᵏ. For mergesort, level k has 2ᵏ pieces of size n/2ᵏ, and the work is n on every level. With log₂ n levels, the total is about n log₂ n.

If the pieces multiply faster than they shrink, the bottom level dominates the total. If the combining work shrinks level by level, the top dominates. If every level costs the same, you add up equal levels.

predict.prompt: If every level of the tree costs the same, how do you get the total?
predict.answer: Multiply the cost of one level by the number of levels.

lessons.title: The three cases
text: When the combining work is n^d (n to the power d), compare a with b^d. If a < b^d, the top of the tree dominates: Θ(n^d). If a = b^d, every level costs the same: Θ(n^d log n). If a > b^d, the bottom dominates: Θ(n^(log_b a)).
Check: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n has a = 4 and b^d = 2, so a is bigger: Θ(n²). T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n has a = 2 = b^d: Θ(n log n). T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n² has a = 2 < 4: Θ(n²).

predict.prompt: In T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n, is a bigger than, equal to, or smaller than b^d?

deeper.title: The fine print
text: This simple form covers work of the shape n^d. The full theorem handles more general work, and has a few conditions. It also does not cover every recurrence, for example when the pieces are not all the same fraction of n.

fieldNotes.title: Why the shortcut exists
fieldNotes.text: Without the shortcut, analysing a divide-and-conquer method means drawing its tree and adding up levels each time. The Master Theorem lets people classify most simple plans from just the three numbers a, b and d.

summary: You wrote plans as recurrences, added up tree levels, and used the three cases from comparing a with b^d.
The old sailor hands over the key. "You asked how much work, and you can answer before running a thing." Next, the same ideas on trees.

levels.title: Treewalker
levels.story: A family tree of ferries is carved on a rock: one first ferry at the top, with children below. Ferry Master Fen asks Kit to read it in three different orders, each useful for a different job.

everyday.scene: A company chart has a boss at the top, managers under the boss, and teams under managers. You want to print a list of everyone.
everyday.question: In what order would you list them?
everyday.answer: It depends: boss first, then each team (preorder), or each team first and the boss last (postorder). The three tree orders do each of these.

lessons.title: A tree and its branches
text: A binary tree has a root at the top. Each node has at most two children, a left one and a right one. A node with no children is a leaf. The height is the number of steps on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

Every branch under a node is itself a smaller tree. That makes trees a natural fit for recursion: to handle a tree, handle the root, then the left tree, then the right tree. Our tree has 7 nodes and height 3.

terms.meaning: Steps on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

predict.prompt: A tree has just one node. What is its height?
predict.answer: 0. The longest path has no steps.

lessons.title: Three ways to walk
text: Preorder visits the node, then its left tree, then its right tree. Inorder visits the left tree, then the node, then the right tree. Postorder visits the left tree, then the right tree, then the node. Only the moment of the visit changes.
On our tree: preorder A, B, D, G, E, C, F; inorder G, D, B, E, A, C, F; postorder G, D, E, B, F, C, A. Each walk visits every node exactly once.

lessons.title: Which walk for which job
text: Preorder is good for copying a tree, because each parent appears before its children. Postorder is good for deleting or totalling a tree, because children are handled before their parent. Inorder, on a search tree (smaller left, bigger right), lists values in sorted order.

Counting the nodes or finding the height is recursive too. The height of a tree is 1 plus the larger of its two subtree heights, and an empty tree has height −1. Each node is visited once, so the work grows with the number of nodes.

predict.prompt: Which walk lists a search tree in sorted order?

deeper.title: No recursion needed?
text: A stack can replace the recursion. A recursive call is really a stack of waiting calls, so every tree walk can be done with an explicit stack.

fieldNotes.title: Trees inside programs
fieldNotes.text: A web page is stored as a tree of elements, and so is a folder structure on a computer. Walking these trees in a chosen order is a daily job for programs.

summary: You learned the words root, leaf and height, walked a tree in preorder, inorder and postorder, and matched each walk to a job.
Fen traces the carvings with a finger. "Boss first, or boss last." The Master's key opens the next rock.

mistake.title: Mixing up the walks
mistake.text: The name says where the node goes: pre means before its subtrees, post means after, and in means between.

levels.title: Sorting Can't Go Faster
levels.story: Printer Pell has a sign over the door: "Nobody can sort by comparing in fewer than about n × log n steps." Kit wants to know how anyone can be so sure of something nobody has found.

everyday.scene: You play twenty questions with only yes-or-no questions, to find which of 1,000 items someone is thinking of.
everyday.question: What is the fewest questions that always works?
everyday.answer: Ten, because 2¹⁰ is just over 1,000: each question at best halves the options. Sorting is the same game, with n! possible orders instead of 1,000 items.

lessons.title: Sorting is a guessing game
text: A sorting method that only compares crates asks yes-or-no questions: is this crate lighter than that one? Draw every possible run of questions as a tree. Each path ends in one final order of the crates.

n crates can be arranged in n! (n factorial) different orders, and the method must be able to end in any of them. So the tree needs at least n! leaves. Three crates have 6 orders, four have 24, five have 120.

terms.meaning: n × (n − 1) × ... × 1: the number of ways to arrange n things.
A final answer: one possible sorted order.

predict.prompt: How many different orders can 4 crates be in?

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 0: Introduction

lessons.title: The least you must ask
text: A tree where each question has two answers has at most 2ᵏ leaves after k questions. To have n! leaves you need 2ᵏ ≥ n!, so k ≥ log₂(n!). The worst-case number of comparisons can never be lower than that.
That works out to 3 comparisons for 3 crates, 7 for 5, 22 for 10, and about 8,530 for 1,000. It is a proof about every possible comparison method, not only the ones we know.

predict.prompt: A comparison sort has 2 answers per question. What is the most leaves it can reach after 3 questions?

lessons.title: Why n log n
text: The value log₂(n!) grows like n × log₂ n. So every method that sorts by comparing needs about n log n comparisons in the worst case. Mergesort uses about that many, so it cannot be beaten by more than a small factor.
The bound is only about comparing. A method that never compares two crates, such as tallying how many crates have each weight, is not covered, and you will meet such methods in Trade Wind Cove.

predict.prompt: Does the n log n bound apply to a method that never compares crates with each other?
predict.answer: No. The bound only covers methods that sort by comparing.

deeper.title: Why n!?
text: n! is at least (n/2) to the power n/2 for large n. Taking log₂ of that gives about (n/2) × log₂(n/2), which grows like n log n.

fieldNotes.title: Proofs about all methods
fieldNotes.text: This is one of the few places in computing where we can say that no method, known or unknown, beats a certain cost, as long as the method sorts only by comparing.

summary: You treated sorting as a guessing game with n! outcomes, worked out the least comparisons for small n, and saw why mergesort's n log n cannot be beaten by any comparison method.
Pell takes down the sign and hangs a new one: "...unless you stop comparing." Trade Wind Cove has that story.

mistake.title: Reading the bound as "sorting is slow"
mistake.text: The bound says comparison sorts need about n log n in the worst case. That is already fast. It also does not rule out methods that sort without comparing.

levels.title: Bonus: Closest Lighthouses II
levels.story: Back on Brute Bay, Captain Ada has hundreds of thousands of lighthouses on a new chart, and checking every pair would take all year. Kit now knows a better way: split the chart in two.

everyday.scene: You are looking for the two closest houses among a million on a map. You cut the map down the middle, find the closest pair on each side, then check only the houses near the cut.
everyday.question: Why only the houses near the cut?
everyday.answer: Anything far from the cut cannot beat the best pair already found on its own side. That is divide and conquer for the closest-pair problem.

lessons.title: Split, solve, combine
text: Sort the points by x, and split them into a left half and a right half. Solve each half by calling the same method on it. A pair of two or three points is the base case, checked by brute force. Then combine: the best pair is either the best on the left, the best on the right, or a pair with one point on each side.
Call the better of the two half-answers d. The crossing pair is the new part, and the clever bit of the method is checking it cheaply.

predict.prompt: The closest pair overall must be in one of which three places?
predict.answer: Inside the left half, inside the right half, or crossing the dividing line.

references.title: Wikipedia: Closest pair of points problem

lessons.title: Only look near the line
text: A crossing pair can only beat d if both points are within d of the dividing line. So keep only the points in the narrow strip around the line. In our chart that strip holds 4 of the 8 points.

text.text: Inside the strip, sort by y. Each point only needs to be compared with the next few points above it: a small constant number. So the combine step costs about n, not n × n.

terms.meaning: The points within distance d of the dividing line.

predict.prompt: Why can a point far from the dividing line be ignored in the combine step?
predict.answer: A crossing pair with that point would be longer than d, so it cannot beat the best pair already found.

deeper.title: Why only a few rivals
text: Within the strip, any point only has a few possible rivals above it, because crowding more points into the same small box would put two of them closer than d on one side.

references.title: Wikipedia: Closest pair of points problem
Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 1: Recursion

lessons.title: The cost
text: The cost follows T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n: two halves, plus about n work to combine. By the Master Theorem that is Θ(n log n). That is a huge saving over the brute-force n × (n − 1) ÷ 2.
For 1,000 points, brute force makes 499,500 comparisons, while n log₂ n is about 9,966. For a million points, brute force needs nearly 500 billion; n log₂ n is about 20 million.

predict.prompt: Does the combine step cost about n or about n × n?
predict.answer: About n: each strip point is compared with only a few others.

references.title: Wikipedia: Closest pair of points problem

fieldNotes.title: Beating brute force
fieldNotes.text: This closest-pair method is a standard example of divide and conquer turning an n × n search into n log n.

source.title: Wikipedia: Closest pair of points problem

summary: You split a chart, solved each half, and checked only a narrow strip for a crossing pair, bringing the cost from about n × n down to about n log n.
Ada rolls up the chart. "A year of checking, down to an afternoon." Brute force found the answer first, and divide and conquer found it fast.

mistake.title: Forgetting the crossing pairs
mistake.text: The best pair of each half is not always the best overall. Without the strip check, a closer pair across the dividing line would be missed.
